wards_summary.note: Each ward is its communities (the ward holding most of each community's area). Rates are per 1,000 residents a year, using residents in the middle of the period, counted the way chosen in Settings. Traffic incidents are placed by their exact location; crime is the Calgary Police Service figure for each ward.

pop_methods.city_actual: City's total, shared by actual growth
pop_methods.city_pace: City's total, one rate for all

population.method_about: The 2021 Census for each community, grown with the homes on the City's current property assessment roll (homes lived in x 2021 people per home). Follows the homes actually built.

city_source.name: Calgary and Region Economic Outlook 2026-2031 (Spring 2026), Table 4 City of Calgary Population Projection, page 19: Total Population (as of April); 2021-2025 estimates, 2026 on forecast (completed January 2026)
city_source.how: The figure for a month is read on a straight line between the April figures before and after it (November 2026: 1,583,200 in April 2026 + 7/12 of the way to 1,608,700 in April 2027 = 1,598,075).

schools.note: Students enrolled in each school inside Calgary (Government of Alberta, Student enrolment by school, authority and grade level). Schools are placed with the City's Schools map. Totals over years count the same schools in every year. Home education and online programs registered at an address here are listed but not counted: their students are taught at home or online, many of them elsewhere in Alberta.

crime.how_to_download: On the Calgary Police page, section "Dashboard data download", click "Download Community Safety Data". Sheet "Community Crime": filter Ward (or Community), Year and Month, and add up "Total Crime".
crime.rounding_note: The police file shows any count from 1 to 5 as 2, for privacy. The police Power BI dashboard shows exact counts, so for a single community and month it can differ from the file (for example Martindale, September 2026: 18 in the file, 22 on the dashboard). Every number in this app is from the file.

rezoning.note: Rezoning (land use redesignation) applications, numbered LOC: a change to what a property may be used for, decided by Council at a public hearing. City of Calgary open data, Land Use Redesignation Applications (33vi-ew4s); placed in a ward or community by their map point. Listed: every application made in the period and every one still open. Hearing dates are on Council agendas, not in the open data.

roadwork.title: 4th Avenue Flyover
roadwork.what: Originally built in 1982, Calgary’s longest bridge structure, the 4th Avenue Flyover needs major repairs and improvements after 42 years of daily service for motorists entering the Downtown. The City is investing $12.5 million to help ensure the bridge continues to be functional, reliable, and in good condition for commuter use for decades to come. Construction will begin in early April 2024 and i

roadwork.title: 14 & 15 Avenue S.W. Mobility Improvements
roadwork.what: We are upgrading infrastructure along 14 and 15 Avenue S. to provide dedicated spaces for walking and wheeling (biking, scootering, and skateboarding). These changes will support community health and wellness, and enhance safety, accessibility, and overall mobility for Calgarians and visitors.

roadwork.title: Blackfoot Trail 9 Ave S.E. Bridge Rehabilitation
roadwork.what: This bridge has been identified for a major rehabilitation to address deterioration. This rehabilitation is expected to improve conditions for motorists and those walking and wheeling along 9 Avenue S.E.

roadwork.title: Mission Bridge Rehabilitation
roadwork.what: Mission Bridge is a vital connection for walking, driving or wheeling in the Mission District. The bridge was built in 1886 and was the first bridge spanning the Elbow River; it opened to traffic in 1915, making it one of Calgary’s oldest bridges. This three-lane bridge spans the Elbow River and connects the communities of Roxboro and Rideau to the Mission District. We’re restoring the Mission Bri

roadwork.title: Crowchild Trail N.W. Paving
roadwork.what: Resurfacing on/off ramps of Crowchild Tr. N.W.  starting at the Shaganappi Trail N.W. ramp and includes on/off ramps at 53 Street N.W., Sarcee Trail N.W., Nose Hill Drive N.W. and Crowfoot Parade N.W.

roadwork.title: Deerfoot Trail widening
roadwork.what: The Province of Alberta is advancing through various stages of the Deerfoot Trail Improvements project. The project is generally split into north Deerfoot Trail which consists of four design/bid/build projects, and south Deerfoot Trail consisting of one large design/build project.

roadwork.title: Country Hills Boulevard NE Widening Project
roadwork.what: This project will widen the section of Country Hills Blvd between Barlow Trail and 36 Street N.E. to help reduce traffic, improve safety, and support future growth.

roadwork.title: Marda Loop Main Street
roadwork.what:
The Marda Loop Main Streets project for 33 and 34 Avenues SW will create safe, thoughtful mobility connections and community spaces through:

- A balance of transportation options, including a focus on pedestrian and cyclist improvements.
- A family-friendly, safe street that focuses on the needs of the community.
- A design that is uniquely “Marda Loop” and reflects its identity.

roadwork.title: Macleod Trail S.E. Median Barriers
roadwork.what:
Included in the project:
- New safety barriers in the median from Shawnessy Blvd S.W. to 99 Ave S.E.
- Road repaving (mill and inlay) from Shawnessy Blvd S.W. to Fish Creek
- Bannister Road Bridge repairs

roadwork.title: Bridgeland Main Streets
roadwork.what: Phase Two of the Bridgeland Main Street project involves operational and streetscape improvements along 1 Avenue N.E. from 4 Street to 11 Street, and along 2 Avenue N.E. between 6 Street N.E. to 10 Street N.E.

roadwork.title: Anderson Road S.E. Improvements
roadwork.what:
Includes improvements along Anderson Rd S.E., from Deerfoot Trail to Macleod Trail.
- Adding a third eastbound lane
- Repaving the road
- Fixing sidewalks, curbs, and wheelchair ramps
- Updating traffic lights at Bonaventure and Acadia Drive
- Putting up new overhead signs

park.basis: A choice, not a standard: distance to the park's edge, 400 m and 800 m.

transit_stop.label: Transit stop
transit_stop.title: Calgary Transit Stops

crowding_spec.unit: transit stops per 1,000 residents within reach

transit_stop.basis: 400 m: Calgary Transit Service Guidelines (May 2025) measure coverage as a 400-metre distance from a bus stop, about a five-minute walk. 800 m is a choice, not from the guidelines.

rec_centre.basis: A choice, not a standard: 2 km and 5 km for facilities that serve several communities.

library.label: Public library

limitations: Straight-line distance, not walking distance: walking routes are longer (curved streets, rivers, rail lines, major roads), so every share is the most generous reading.
The City's inventory only: school, developer, condominium, community association and private amenities are not counted.
A transit stop is not a service level: how often buses come is not measured.
The size and condition of amenities are not measured: each playground counts as one, whatever its size.
Park crowding counts each park's whole area, natural areas and regional parks included, so homes near a very large park (Nose Hill, Fish Creek) show very high hectares per 1,000 residents.
Rental units are partly estimated: purpose-built rental buildings count as their units, from building permits or, where no permit matches, estimated from assessed value.

Children and residents are spread evenly over the homes of each community, from the population model's estimates (the 2021 Census plus modelled growth), not counted. The crowding figures will be firmed up with the 2026 Census age data in 2027.
New communities on the city's edge are naturally farther from shared facilities (recreation centres, libraries), some planned for later phases.
Community centre data needs checking: several large communities show no community centre within 800 m, which may mean community association halls are missing from the City's list.

limits: The forecast is the City's, for new communities only (its seven suburban sectors); growth in established communities (infill, redevelopment) is not in it and is not added here.

The City forecasts by sector, not by community. Each sector's figure is shared among its new communities by the homes built there in the last five years: a community just opening up (or one about to run out of land) will get more (or less) than this share.
The forecast's 2026 homes are added in full; homes built early in 2026 may already be in today's count.

Amenities in 2030 are shown two ways: today's only (nothing new opens), and today's plus what is already planned: park land zoned as reserve in new communities that is not yet a City park, and libraries, recreation centres and community centres being built and due by 2030. Planned playgrounds and new transit stops are not in any published list, so they are not added; a reserve may hold a school as well as a park.

New residents are spread over a community's homes like today's residents: new homes on the growing edge are often farther from amenities than the community's average, so 2030 crowding there may be worse than shown.
Children: the community's share of children today, applied to its new residents.

referendum.question: Question 1: Do you support the Government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?

Question 2: Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially-funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

Question 3: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially-funded social support programs?

Question 4: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family's use of the health care and education systems?

Question 5: Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

Question 6: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King's Bench and Appeal courts?
Question 7: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

Question 8: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?

Question 9: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province's laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province's laws and federal laws conflict?

Question 10: Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

Question 3: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially-funded social support programs?

Question 4: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family's use of the health care and education systems?

Question 5: Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

Question 6: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King's Bench and Appeal courts?
Question 7: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

Question 8: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?

Question 9: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province's laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province's laws and federal laws conflict?

Question 10: Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

areas.note: Residents and who lives here: each community's residents today (the count chosen in Settings) times the share of the community inside the division or district, with its 2021 Census mix. Wards, mayor and referendum figures for a district are residents-weighted estimates. Swing to flip: the uniform swing from the winner to the runner-up that would tie the last result (half the margin).

notes: Residents are counted with Growth model (chosen in Settings): The 2021 Census for each community, grown with the homes on the City's current property assessment roll (homes lived in x 2021 people per home). Follows the homes actually built. The 2021 Census count is shown beside it. Rates per 1,000 residents a year use residents in the middle of each period.
Infrastructure reports are the 21 roads, water and sewer, and parks and trees service types used in the 311 equity study.
The City publishes most 311 requests at their community's centre point, not their address, so 311 is mapped by community, not by street.
Traffic incidents are the City's reported incidents with exact locations, inside the City boundary.

Crime and disorder by community come from the Calgary Police Service community safety data (the data behind its Community Safety Dashboard), published every quarter by month. Incidents without a location are left out. The Crime Severity Index (Statistics Canada) compares Calgary with other cities each year.
